answer:
**Natural-language hypothesis (deliverable):**

"In the NLSY79 1989 sample (ages 24–32), age has no meaningful influence on the likelihood of DISSAVED = 1: after adjusting for gender, income, race/ethnicity, and BMI, the predicted probability of dissaving is essentially flat across the age range — ≈0.29 (95% CI 0.27–0.31) at age 25 vs ≈0.31 (95% CI 0.29–0.33) at age 30, a difference of only ~1–2 percentage points — with at most a weak, statistically non-significant non-monotonic hump peaking near age 30 rather than any monotonic increase or decline."

**Optional explicit hypothesis string:**

H_age: AGE has no significant association with P(DISSAVED=1) over ages 24–32; model-adjusted dissaving probability is flat at ≈0.29–0.31 (age 25 vs 30: +1.6 pp; age 24 vs 32: +1.9 pp), with at most a mild hump near age 30 — after conditioning on GENDER, INCOME, BLACK, HISPANIC, BMI and excluding mean-imputed records (joint age test n.s.).

**Optional workflow note:**

Loaded data/nls_bmi_processed.csv (12,686×9; no explicit NaN). Flagged a mean-imputation artifact: 31% of INCOME and ~20% of BMI sit exactly at their column means; those artificially filled rows almost never dissave (≈11% for imputed income, ≈4% for imputed BMI vs ≈29% fully observed) and are increasingly common at older ages (age 24: 272 imputed-income rows → age 31: 646), which also explains all 2,151 exact duplicate rows (max multiplicity 216). On the raw data this produces a spurious, significant decline in dissaving with age (AGE −0.047/yr, p<0.001), which vanishes once the imputation indicators are controlled (AGE p=0.66).

Primary analysis: 8,425 complete-case rows (observed income and BMI; 11 implausible BMI≥80 excluded) — logistic regression DISSAVED ~ centered AGE + AGE² + MALE + INCOME + BLACK + HISPANIC + BMI. Diagnostics: AGE β=+0.0116 (SE=0.0109, p=0.285, 95% CI −0.010 to +0.033); AGE² β=−0.0032 (SE=0.0050, p=0.521, 95% CI −0.013 to +0.007); adding AGE² does not improve fit (AIC 10198.4 → 10200.0; LRT for AGE² p=0.52; pseudo-R²=0.0025); joint Wald test of AGE & AGE²: χ²=1.96, p=0.376; average marginal effect ≈ +0.3 pp/year. Predicted probabilities are flat (age 24: 0.286, 25: 0.293, 28: 0.306, 30: 0.309, 32: 0.305) with overlapping 95% CIs (see prediction_grid.csv). Age-band descriptive rates on complete rows: 24–25: 28.4%, 26–28: 28.8%, 29–31: 30.1%, 32: 30.2% (vs 25.5/25.4/22.5/20.9 on all rows — the raw decline is the artifact). Sensitivity on all 12,675 rows with IMP_INC/IMP_BMI indicators: age terms n.s. (AGE p=0.656, AGE² p=0.421) while both indicators are strongly significant (p<0.001). Robustness with log1p(INCOME): age terms n.s. (p=0.873 / p=0.563). Conclusion is thus stable across complete-case, all-rows+indicators, and log-income specifications. Interpretive limits: cross-sectional (age at 1989 also encodes cohort), binary outcome (no amounts), and dissaving is only a proxy for time preference.

payload.hypothesis: AGE has no meaningful association with P(DISSAVED=1) over ages 24-32: adjusted dissaving probability is flat at ≈0.29-0.31 (age 25 vs 30: +1.6 pp; age 24 vs 32: +1.9 pp), at most a non-significant mild hump near age 30, conditioning on GENDER, INCOME, BLACK, HISPANIC, BMI, and excluding mean-imputed records (joint AGE test χ2=1.96, p=0.38).
payload.workflow: Complete-case (n=8425) logistic regression of DISSAVED on centered AGE+AGE2+MALE+INCOME+BLACK+HISPANIC+BMI; primary on rows with observed income & BMI (BMI<80); sensitivity on all 12675 rows with imputation indicators (imp values at exact column mean) and log-income robustness; predicted probabilities at covariate means with delta-method 95% CI; the raw-data age decline (AGE -0.047, p<0.001) is shown to be an artifact of mean-imputed rows that almost never dissave and concentrate at older ages.
